articles.title: Vets can diagnose bluetongue virus to cut test waiting times
articles.summary: The government announces the change in approach as the virus continues to spread in the UK.
articles.body:
Vets will now be able to diagnose bluetongue virus in livestock so farmers do not have to wait for confirmed test results under changes announced by the government.

The potentially deadly virus, which affects sheep and cattle as well as other animals, continues to spread with confirmed cases on 1,048 farms in the UK - more than half are in Devon and Cornwall.

Farmers previously needed to wait for samples to be sent to a laboratory to confirm bluetongue but the government said vets would now be able to diagnose the disease after examining the animals.

UK deputy chief veterinary officer Ele Brown said: "Bluetongue is widely circulating in England and our approach needs to keep pace."

How bluetongue virus exploded in the South West

What is the potentially deadly bluetongue virus?

Farmers grieving over bluetongue urged to talk

The deputy chief vet added: "Private vets are well placed to recognise signs of the diseases, and this change will mean farmers can get a diagnosis more quickly.

"Vaccination is the best tool available to help protect susceptible livestock, so I absolutely continue to urge farmers to speak to their vet about vaccinating their herd or flock."

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it had set up a new online system allowing vets to report confirmed cases.

It said the changes would "mean fewer straightforward cases need to wait for laboratory results, giving farmers an answer sooner and helping them take quicker action to protect livestock".

A new heat map has also been published so farmers can see where suspected and confirmed cases of bluetongue were being reported, said Defra.

Spread mainly by midge bites, the virus was confirmed in a sheep in Cornwall in September 2025 .

This strain was introduced into Cornwall from midges blown in wind from northern France but scientists believe the virus likely spread rapidly after overwintering in parts of the UK.

The outbreak has hit the agriculture sector hard and some farmers fear it will have a lasting impact .

Jerry Sanders-Carr, who runs Exe Valley Lamb, near Exeter, said he had lost 15% of his sheep to the virus.

"Talking to some of the guys who've been going out picking up large numbers of dead animals every morning, some of these guys I'm sure there's going to be a lasting impact on them," he said.

Mark Walter, who farms in Milton Damerel in north Devon, feared 40% of his lambs could be born stillborn or with disabilities because of bluetongue.

He added: "All we were doing is jabbing sheep day and night. The poor sheep, it was horrendous for them."

articles.title: Jewish campus life at a ‘crossing point’ as students weigh antisemitism risks, new report shows
articles.summary: Alums for Campus Fairness names the 10 most concerning and 10 most supportive campuses for Jewish students in its new 2025-26 campus climate report.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — The difference between a hostile and a supportive campus for Jewish students may come down to how administrators act when tensions rise, according to a new report. Alums for Campus Fairness (ACF) released its 2025-26 Campus Climate Brief in which it names the 10 most concerning and 10 most supportive campuses for Jewish students, along with a few "honorable mentions" in both categories. "The schools that get it right understand their role and understand that they have an obligation to support all students, including Jewish students and Zionist students," ACF Executive Director Avi Gordon told Fox News Digital. "And I think those schools are flourishing, they’re welcoming, and it’s a place that’s desirable for certainly within the Jewish and pro-Israel community." To evaluate each of the schools profiled in the report, ACF used five criteria: incident records, the institution's response to antisemitism, anti-Israel organizing, Jewish life on campus and an evaluation of the legal and structural environment. The report found 14 concerning campuses and 17 strong campuses across 17 states. BIPARTISAN DUO LAUNCHES CONGRESSIONAL CAUCUS TO CONFRONT ANTISEMITISM AT COLLEGES The 10 most concerning campuses in the report are Middlebury College, The New School, DePaul University, Smith College, Sarah Lawrence College, San Francisco State University (SFSU), University of Texas at Dallas, University of California, Berkeley, Oberlin College and George Mason University. Alums for Campus Fairness also gave "honorable mentions" to the City University of New York System, University of Washington, Occidental College and Pitzer College. ACF profiled each of the schools, detailing antisemitic incidents, institutional responses — or lack thereof — and anti-Israel organizing, among other factors. For Middlebury College, ACF cited the university's Hillel chapter renaming itself "The Jewish Association at Middlebury," after "an attempted disaffiliation from Hillel international." "Whatever the internal politics, the fact that national Hillel affiliation is contested at all reflects how thoroughly anti-Zionist sentiment has penetrated the campus's Jewish institutional life," ACF's report read. According to the report, the Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP) chapter at the New School advertised a "Vigil for Martyr Yahya Sinwar," referring to the deceased leader of Hamas. ACF noted that the group continued to promote the event even after Meta removed the original post. At UC Berkeley, "wanted" posters targeting Jewish UC regents appeared in September 2025. Then, in November 2025, "Kill all Zionists" was spray-painted in Berkeley graduate housing. The report also noted that UC Berkeley was sued by the Justice Department in February 2026 for maintaining "an antisemitic hostile work environment." SFSU was included on ACF's list of most concerning campuses because of what the organization described as a broader anti-Zionist culture embedded in the university. The report cited the hosting of Mahmoud Khalil by the university's Race and Resistance Studies department and the General Union of Palestine Students. However, SFSU disputed ACF's characterization, with Director of Communications Bobby King telling Fox News Digital via email that "SFSU has made combatting antisemitism a University priority." King pointed to SFSU's 2022 partnership with SF Hillel, Hillel International and the Academic Engagement Network "to implement a program developed by the latter two organizations designed to combat antisemitism on college campuses." In a recent JWeekly article, Roger Feigelson, executive director of the San Francisco Hillel that serves SFSU, called the university "a role model for how to fight antisemitism on college campuses." OPINION: CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM IS AN AMERICA FIRST ISSUE. ALUMNI MUST STAY IN THE FIGHT. articles.title: Russian strikes kill two in Kyiv as Moscow targets capital’s fuel stations
articles.summary: Second day of strikes on fuel stations suggest a new campaign focused on civilian areas in the Ukrainian capital.
articles.body:
Russian drone attacks on two fuel stations in Kyiv have killed two people and injured others, as Moscow continues to target civilian areas.

They were struck early on Friday within ten minutes of each other in the capital’s Obolonskyi and Dniprovskyi districts, shortly after emergency sirens rang out, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a statement.

Russia also targeted fuel stations in Kyiv on Thursday, suggesting a new campaign focused on civilian areas in the capital. Ukrainian authorities have warned people to avoid filling up when air raid sirens sound.

One person died at the scene of one of the attacks, Klitschko said, while the other died in hospital. Six people required hospital treatment.

While fuel stations near the eastern and southern battle lines have been hit regularly for months, authorities have long warned that the attacks could extend to the capital as an intimidation strategy.

Russia and Ukraine both deny targeting civilians as the conflict – started with Moscow’s invasion in February 2022 – has developed into a series of daily attacks with missiles and drones.

Other Russian drone strikes overnight hit near a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, leaving five dead and 67 injured, while a mother and son were injured in Zaporizhzhia when a drone hit an apartment building and a mall.

Ukraine’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, declared Friday a day of mourning.

On Thursday, he condemned Russia for attacking civilian areas in a bid to sow fear.

“Russia is systematically attacking places where it knows people will be spending their time going about their daily lives, seeking to maximise casualties, spread fear and put pressure on Ukrainian society,” he stated.

Ukraine unleashed its own large-scale drone attack through the night, with Russia’s Ministry of Defence reporting that its forces shot down 777 drones in 16 regions.

Two people were killed and three injured in Tula, to the south of Moscow, local authorities reported.

articles.title: The dystopian legal architecture of the ‘war on terror’ must be dismantled
articles.summary: A quarter-century after 9/11, we are still living under the security order it unleashed.
articles.body:
A protest movement has been proscribed as a terrorist organisation, thereby criminalising support for those enduring a genocide rather than any act of violence. Migrants are being held in detention facilities modelled on the very practices documented at Guantanamo Bay, and some are even being sent to the Cuban detention camp itself. Surveillance infrastructure once built to monitor “terrorism” has quietly been turned on Palestine solidarity protesters instead. None of this sits at the edges of the law, straining against it or slipping past its limits. It sits comfortably within laws written 25 years ago, doing precisely what they were written to do.

The legal architecture assembled after 9/11 was sold to the public as an emergency response to a single, unrepeatable day. A quarter of a century later, it has not been rolled back, nor even meaningfully questioned. It has simply become permanent, its reach extending steadily beyond anything its original architects would have needed to justify at the time.

It is worth resisting, too, the instinct to treat 9/11 as the origin of this story. The hostility that the “war on terror” eventually gave a name to was already established Western policy long before that morning arrived; 9/11 did not invent the idea that certain populations could be treated as a security problem before they were treated as human beings; it simply furnished that idea with a name, a legal framework, and a budget without limit. Read the last 25 years as a continuation of something older, rather than an aberration that began with a single attack, and the years since start to make a different kind of sense.

Seen that way, the throughline is difficult to miss. What began as indefinite detention at Guantanamo Bay has grown into the working infrastructure of a far broader security state. The same legal tools have been carried forward rather than retired, first used to justify holding men without charge, then to designate a protest movement a “terrorist” organisation for the positions it holds, and now to run immigration enforcement on a national security logic drawn directly from the “war on terror”. Each expansion has been presented, in turn, as a departure, a special case, an exception demanded by the moment. Yet this is what a permanent security architecture does once it is built: it merely shifts to its next target.

The case that shows this most starkly is not one of prosecution but of detention that never required one. Mansoor Adayfi was held at Guantanamo for nearly 15 years without ever being charged with a crime, and has written of treatment no human being should have to endure. In one of the camp’s more telling episodes, he opened a boxed meal to find the words “we will never forget, we will never forgive” scrawled on the inside of the box. When he wrote back demanding justice rather than vengeance, the camp administration answered with food punishment and solitary confinement, on the grounds that his message amounted to a death threat.

Guantanamo never needed a conviction to hold him for a decade and a half. It needed only the architecture built after 9/11, and the presumption embedded within it that a man like him could be treated as a suspect indefinitely, without the state ever having to prove why. What Guantanamo demonstrated, in other words, was not simply a place but a method: that indefinite suspicion could be built into law and would hold, that a population could be designated a security risk and processed accordingly, with no charge required and no real accounting demanded. It is that method, not the camp itself, that has since travelled.

It is difficult to look at a proscribed protest movement or a migrant held in conditions that directly echo those at Guantanamo and not recognise the same architecture at work. The same presumption, applied differently, produced convictions elsewhere that later could not survive scrutiny: one that kept Hamid Hayat imprisoned for 14 years, secured through coerced statements, and another that kept Dr Ali al-Tamimi imprisoned or confined for 20 years, based entirely on protected speech and overturned by a US appellate court only this year. Guantanamo did not even need that pretence. It needed only the architecture itself.

Twenty-five years is long enough to know that these laws were never temporary, and long enough to know they were never going to correct themselves. The only response still worth taking seriously is to abolish them.

articles.title: Is Your Heated Workout Ruining Your Hair? Here’s What Hair Experts Say | NBC Selected
articles.summary: Heat, sweat and humidity during heated workouts may damage your hair and scalp. Here’s how dermatologists recommend prepping your hair before and after.
articles.body: For me, very few workouts feel as fulfilling as a heated one. But as a beauty editor, I’m constantly worrying about how the excess heat and sweat affects my skin and hair (including the slicked-back buns I wear to keep hair out of my face). Will my scalp be a wreck after a few weeks of steady hot yoga? Should I cancel my hot Pilates membership to avoid a head of breakage, split ends and dandruff? Fortunately, you don’t have to choose between heated workouts or healthy hair; you just have to tweak your routine to avoid damage in the first place. I spoke to board-certified dermatologists and hairstylists about how exactly heated workouts are affecting your hair and what you can do to keep your hair breakage-free. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What do heated workouts do to your hair? Heated workouts can be tricky for hair because you’re combining higher temperatures, humidity and more sweat than you might experience during a typical workout. While routine heated workouts don’t usually expose your hair to temperatures comparable to heated styling tools like a flat iron or curling iron, they can still cause some damage. “A hot yoga room is not the same thermal insult as putting a 400-degree flat iron directly against the hair shaft. For most people, the bigger issue is the combination of sweat, humidity, tension, washing and repeated styling afterward,” says Dr. Kseniya Kobets, director of cosmetic dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. “Sweat itself isn’t inherently bad for the hair or scalp, but when it sits there for a prolonged period, the combination of moisture, salt, oil and heat can create buildup and leave the scalp feeling itchy, irritated or uncomfortable,” says Dr. Alexandra Bowles, a board-certified dermatologist at Mona Dermatology. For people who are already prone to dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis, that warm, moist environment can sometimes make symptoms worse. “The biggest mistake I see is immediately putting sweaty hair into a bun and leaving it there,” says Rogerio Cavalcante, hairstylist and founder of Brazil Edition. “The scalp stays damp, while the combination of sweat, heat and friction can leave the roots feeling dirty and the lengths frizzy or dry.” The hair itself can also experience damage: “As sweat dries, the salt left behind can make hair feel drier, rougher or more brittle, particularly if it is color-treated, chemically processed or already dry,” says Bowles. Humidity can also cause the hair shaft to swell, which might cause more frizz and changes in texture after a heated workout. Your hair may start to feel rougher or drier, look frizzier or duller, and become more prone to tangling and breakage. “I’d think of it less as the workout heat directly ‘damaging’ the hair and more as repeated exposure creating conditions that can make already vulnerable hair more susceptible to damage,” says Bowles. Best products to protect your hair before and after a heated workout Best leave-in conditioner This leave-in conditioner spray comes recommended by Bowles, who recommends applying a light layer through the ends (rather than the roots) before class to keep it moisturized. It’s also a favorite of NBC Selected associate social media editor Caitlin Cusack, who uses it to protect her hair when she’s out in the sun or exposed to heat. “My hair is on the drier side, especially in the summer, and this product instantly gives hydration and thermal protection, leaving it feeling soft and smooth,” says Cusack. It also helps tame frizz, detangle hair and prevent color from fading, according to the brand. Plus, it has moisturizers like aloe vera and panthenol to keep hair soft and shiny. Best gentle shampoo When washing your hair after a heated workout, experts recommend using a gentle shampoo to remove sweat, oil, and buildup without leaving the hair feeling stripped. Bowles recommends this one from Vanicream because it doesn’t have common irritants like fragrance, dyes and parabens. Great for all hair types and especially for sensitive scalps, this shampoo helps remove flakes and buildup from conditioners and styling products. Best hair mask A moisturizing hair mask, like this one from Briogeo, can be helpful for hair that’s particularly dry, color-treated or chemically processed, says Bowles. I love using this mask on my dry, fine hair because it hydrates without weighing it down or causing it to feel greasy. I use it once or twice a week to keep my hair moisturized, control frizz and detangle, especially after several heated workouts in a row. Best for texture Anti-humidity hair products can be very helpful for controlling the swelling and frizz that occur when curly or porous hair is exposed to a humid environment (like a workout class) and sweat, says Kobets. “They’re great if your main concern is frizz or changes in texture because they can help reduce the amount of moisture moving in and out of the hair shaft,” says Bowles. You can use this Amika spray on your hair prior to your heated workout class to control frizz and moisture, plus it acts as a heat protectant up to 450 degrees. The spray also has sea buckthorn, which is rich in fatty acids and antioxidants to nourish and strengthen both your hair and scalp, according to the brand. Keep in mind this is more of a styling tool than something you need for the health of your hair, so if heated workouts are a regular part of your routine, put more emphasis on gentle cleansing, conditioning, minimizing tension and friction, and limiting unnecessary heat styling, says Bowles. Best for heavy sweaters If you sweat heavily and also use a lot of dry shampoo or styling products, Bowles recommends using this Neutrogena clarifying shampoo every one to two weeks to remove buildup. However, you don’t necessarily need a special “detox” shampoo just because you work out often, and you shouldn’t use it every day because it may be too drying for some hair types, says Bowles. Best for dry hair Seen is one of our favorite hair care brands, and it’s one that Kobets recommends for sensitive and acne-prone scalps. This conditioner moisturizes, softens and strengthens hair while reducing frizz and breakage from your heated workouts. It’s deeply moisturizing, so it’s especially great for those with dry hair. The brand recommends focusing on the mid-lengths and ends of your hair and leaving it on for two to three minutes before rinsing. How can you prep your hair before a heated workout? Ultimately, heated workouts aren’t necessarily bad for your hair — it really comes down to how you care for your scalp and hair before and after. These are some expert tips to protect your hair prior to your workout: Secure hair loosely without putting too much tension on the hairline. “A loose braid, low ponytail or bun with a soft scrunchie is generally better than a very tight ponytail,” says Bowles. “If you sweat heavily around the hairline, a soft, moisture-wicking headband can also help absorb some of that moisture.” Alternate where you place your ponytail, bun or part so you’re not repeatedly putting traction on the exact same areas, (especially around your temples and hairline), says Kobets.Apply a small amount of lightweight leave-in conditioner or conditioning serum through the mid-lengths and ends to help reduce moisture loss and friction, especially if your hair is dry, curly, color-treated or prone to breakage.Avoid applying heavy oils, pomades, waxes or other thick products directly to your scalp before a heated workout because it can contribute to buildup as you sweat. “The goal is really to protect the more vulnerable lengths and ends of the hair without creating another layer of product on the scalp,” says Bowles. What should you do to your hair post-heated workout? Here’s what experts recommend doing after and in between your heated workouts: Right after your workout, let your hair down and your scalp dry out as soon as possible. If you have access to a blow dryer, use cool or low heat and focus primarily on the roots, says Cavalcante. “Even if you’re not washing your hair, getting the moisture out of the scalp makes a huge difference in how fresh the hair looks and feels,” he says.Once your scalp is dry, use a small amount of dry shampoo at the roots. “I always recommend using dry shampoo on dry hair rather than spraying it directly onto a sweaty scalp. Apply it in sections, give it a moment to absorb, and then massage or brush it through so you don’t end up with too much product sitting at the roots,” says Cavalcante.When sweat makes your hair feel dry, tangled or frizzy, use a very small amount of lightweight leave-in conditioner to bring softness back without weighing it down. If you sweat heavily, though, sometimes you’ll simply have to wash your hair. “You don’t want to keep layering dry shampoo and styling products over a scalp that needs to be cleansed,” says Cavalcante. “In that case, use a gentle shampoo and concentrate it on your scalp, letting the shampoo rinse through the lengths rather than aggressively cleansing the entire hair.”Pay attention to the products you’re using between washes, especially if you workout often. Look for products with conditioning ingredients like glycerin, hyaluronic acid, panthenol and ceramides, as well as emollients, silicones or lightweight oils. “The goal isn’t necessarily to create an impermeable barrier. You want to decrease friction and moisture loss without coating the scalp so heavily that you trap additional sweat and buildup,” says Kobets. That’s why you should avoid heavy oils, creams and too much dry shampoo, which can build up quickly when combined with sweat. Meet our hair care experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Kseniya Kobets is a board-certified dermatologist and director of cosmetic dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care in Elmsford, New York.Dr. Alexandra Bowles is a board-certified dermatologist at Mona Dermatology in Cincinnati, Ohio.Rogerio Cavalcante is a hairstylist and founder of Brazil Edition hair care. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m an editor at NBC Selected who has covered beauty topics, including skin and hair care, for over six years. I’m also an avid heated workout fan and attend hot yoga and Pilates classes at least three times a week. For this article, I spoke to dermatologists and hairstylists about how to protect your hair and scalp before and after a heated workout. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Meet Neha Blunt: The 13-year-old New Jersey coder whose water-saving campaign has reached 1 million people and helped save an estimated 20 million gallons
articles.summary: US News: At 13, Neha Blunt is using code, creativity and community action to tackle one of the world’s most urgent environmental challenges. The New Jersey stu.
articles.body: At 13, Neha Blunt is using code, creativity and community action to tackle one of the world’s most urgent environmental challenges. The New Jersey student created Water Saver, a web application that turns everyday conservation into an interactive challenge, helping households track their water use and make practical changes. Her wider campaign has educated more than 1 million people worldwide, encouraged over 100,000 residents to change daily habits and contributed to an estimated 20 million gallons of water savings. As reported by Action for Nature and South Jersey Media, Neha’s project began with a simple belief that every drop counts, then grew into an international youth-led campaign combining software development, public education and grassroots organising. Read on to know more about her:A question with a global answerNeha’s work began with a familiar environmental problem. Water is essential for drinking, food production, sanitation and ecosystems, yet much of it is wasted through habits that feel too small to matter. A tap left running, an unnecessarily long shower or a lawn watered during rain may seem insignificant on its own. Multiplied across thousands of households, however, those small actions can add up to millions of gallons.The challenge is not always a lack of concern. Many people want to conserve water but do not know how much they use or which changes would make the biggest difference. Traditional conservation messages often rely on warnings, statistics or seasonal reminders. Neha took a different approach. She used technology to make water saving more visible, measurable and engaging.Her campaign reflects a wider understanding of environmental behaviour. People are more likely to change when they receive clear information, practical choices and feedback about their progress. When conservation becomes something users can monitor and share, Water Saver gives households a way to see their individual efforts as part of a larger collective movement.Building Water Saver from the ground upNeha spent seven months teaching herself code to build Water Saver, an online platform that turns conservation into a game. Instead of lecturing people to use less water, her dashboard lets users set goals, take pledges, and track daily habits. Because water use normally disappears down the drain without a thought, the app makes those hidden routines easy to see and measure.In spring 2023, she grew the project into a full grassroots campaign. Neha partnered with schools and community groups, ditching dense environmental jargon for simple, practical actions. Anyone—from a neighborhood in New Jersey to users clear across the globe—could jump in and participate. That straightforward approach paid off: the project reached over one million people worldwide and moved more than 100,000 residents to fix their daily water habits.How small changes create large savingsThe estimated 20 million gallons of water saved through the campaign did not come from one dramatic intervention. It resulted from many participants making repeated changes in their homes and routines. That is an important part of Neha’s message. Conservation does not always require expensive equipment or major construction. Behavioural changes can make a meaningful difference when enough people participate. Households may reduce consumption by shortening showers, turning off taps while brushing teeth, repairing leaks, running dishwashers and washing machines only with full loads, and adjusting outdoor watering. Some actions save a little water each time, others stop the constant loss of water from broken plumbing or inefficient irrigation.The value of a campaign like Water Saver is that it moves people from awareness to action. A person may already know that water is valuable, but an interactive challenge can provide the prompt needed to change a routine. When progress is recorded and shared, participants can also see that their efforts are contributing to something larger than their own utility bill.The role of coding in environmental actionNeha’s project shows how programming can be applied to environmental problems without requiring a large company or government agency. Software can organise information, encourage participation and make complex systems easier to navigate. Coding in Water Saver is a bridge between environmental education and personal behavior. The project also points out the necessity of designing technology for people. An app can have the right information, but it won’t make a difference if it is difficult to use or disconnected from everyday life. Neha was interested in making conservation interactive and accessible, and providing users with a reason to return and continue their efforts. Her example may be especially inspiring to other young people. Environmental action doesn’t have to take one traditional route. A student interested in coding can develop a conservation tool. Someone drawn to art can create public messaging. Another young person might organise a local repair event or help schools reduce waste. The common thread is using available skills to address a real problem.Recognition from Action for NatureNeha’s work was recognised by Action for Nature through its 2026 International Young Eco-Hero Awards. She received third place for creating the Water Saver web app and leading a campaign that has reportedly saved more than 20 million gallons of water while educating over 1 million people. The recognition places her among young environmental leaders whose projects combine initiative with measurable impact. Awards do not create the work, but they can help expand its reach. The publicity could attract more users to the app, connect Neha with potential partners and encourage other students to create their own solutions. The award also represents a broader shift in the perception of young people’s leadership on environmental issues. Young people are not just participating in cleanups or awareness drives. They are writing software, analyzing data, developing campaigns and influencing public behavior. Their age may limit their access to some resources but it doesn’t limit their ability to identify problems and find practical solutions.Making conservation a habit for allWater conservation is most effective when it becomes a part of everyday life rather than a short-term response to drought.Neha’s campaign is trying to bring about this kind of lasting change by making water saving a collective habit. When participants track their actions and see others doing the same, conservation becomes social as well as personal. That community element matters because individual households often feel powerless when faced with global environmental problems. A person may wonder whether one shorter shower can make a difference. A campaign can show how thousands of similar decisions combine into a measurable outcome. The estimated 20 million gallons associated with Water Saver provides a powerful answer. The number represents the accumulated effect of many ordinary choices. It does not suggest that software alone can solve water scarcity, but it demonstrates that behaviour change can be an important part of a broader strategy involving infrastructure, policy, conservation planning and responsible management.What comes nextNeha’s campaign has room to grow as more people use digital tools to understand household resource consumption. Future versions could include more detailed tracking, regional water information, school challenges and partnerships with utilities or community organisations. The basic idea could also be adapted to energy, waste or other environmental goals.The most important next step might be keeping participants engaged after the initial challenge is over. Long-term conservation depends on sustaining habits, updating goals and showing users that their actions continue to matter. Ongoing education and community support can help to stop early enthusiasm from fading. At 13, Neha is just starting out on her journey as a coder and environmental advocate. Already her Water Saver project shows a mature understanding of how technology can underpin public action. She has taken a resource that people often use without thinking about and made it something of attention, measurement and shared responsibility.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Police search for owner of teddy with human ashes left on train
articles.summary: Transport police say they have no information about the passenger who brought the urn on board.
articles.body:
Police are hoping to reunite a teddy and an urn containing human remains with its owner after it was left on a train in Aberdeen.

The decorative vase, which is cradled in the arms of the brown cuddly toy, is thought to have been handed in to lost property at Aberdeen station after arriving on an LNER service from London Kings Cross.

The small, red urn is wrapped in artificial purple and white flowers and has a golden ribbon tied around its top.

It has been held in storage by ScotRail for about four months, but officers from British Transport Police (BTP) said they had "no further information" about its previous owner.

They asked anyone with information about the urn, or the loved ones it belongs to, to contact them .

BTP officer Gary Herning said: "The urn appears to contain human ashes or remains and will clearly be of enormous sentimental value to someone.

"Unfortunately, we have no further information on where the owner may have boarded or alighted during the journey."

articles.title: Are Colored Mascaras Safe for Your Eyes? I Asked Eye Doctors to Find Out
articles.summary: Colored mascaras have been on our feeds all summer, but are they really safe to use on your eyes? I asked ophthalmologists to find out about the potential risks and how to avoid them.
articles.body: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends on our timelines, like whether honey is good for your skin. Colored mascara has been one of summer’s most ubiquitous trends, and it’s showing no signs of stopping as we approach fall — whether on my Instagram explore page, scrolling my TikTok feed, or even out IRL, it’s been impossible to miss. Brands are launching their own versions in shades like blue, purple, green and more. However, as someone whose eyes are sensitive to makeup like mascara and eyeliner, it got me wondering: are colored mascaras really safe for your eyes? I talked to Dr. Diana Zanoni-Potts, a board-certified ophthalmologist at Dignity Medical Aesthetics & Wellness, and Dr. Manjot Gill, a board-certified ophthalmologist, retina specialist and the Vice Chair of Clinical Performance for Ophthalmology in Northwestern’s Feinberg School of Medicine, to find out everything you should know before trying this trend. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Are colored mascaras safe? In a word: yes. According to our experts, when a mascara is made by a reputable brand that uses FDA-compliant colorants (specifically those approved for the eye area), it can generally be considered safe. “What makes colored mascara unique is how tightly the FDA regulates which pigments can be used near the eyes,” says Zanoni-Potts. According to her, the colorful, synthetic dyes that are used in lipsticks and blushes are prohibited from being used in eye products, due to the risk of the looser particles getting into the eye. This is the real safety concern, more so than the mascara’s color, she says — glitter or shimmer formulas with loose, chunky particles can flake off into the eye and cause corneal irritation or abrasion. The other key safety risk is expired mascara, which she describes as “anything used past roughly three months.” Expired mascara can pose a risk of bacterial contamination, since it’s applied in a moist environment that can promote the growth of bacteria and fungi every time you open the tube, says Gill. To avoid this, make sure the mascara is within its shelf life before using. The best colored mascaras to shop Both ophthalmologists suggest shopping colored mascaras from trusted brands that produce clean beauty products, which are formulated “without many of the most concerning chemicals,” says Gill. Below, I gathered a few top-rated colored mascara options to shop from brands like Ilia, Kosas, Tower28 and more. Ilia is one of our favorite clean beauty brands, and this brown mascara was my everyday go-to for over a year when it was initially released. The formula is smooth and thin without being too clunky, and is made with shea butter to condition your lashes while wearing, along with beeswax to define lashes without clumping, according to the brand. I also love how well the deep brown color compliments my brown eyes. This mascara from Kosas is a lengthening mascara and lash serum all in one, according to the brand. It includes peptides, which helps to grow lashes longer in six to eight weeks, and has a curved brush to make sure every lash can be easily reached. The mascara is also safe for sensitive eyes, and can be layered with added coats at any point during the day without flaking, according to the brand. Tower 28 is another NBC Selected-favorite brand, and this mascara has a vegan formula that’s been tested by ophthalmologists. It’s fragrance-free and resistant to smudging and transfer, and includes a dual-sided brush for both volume and length, according to the brand. It’s also formulated to be easy to wash off (despite the water-resistant formula), and is safe for sensitive eyes. Essence’s Lash Princess line is my drugstore go-to and has been since college. The conical brush is great for separating and lengthening my lashes, which makes them look longer and thicker without over-clumping or flaking. It’s also part of Ulta’s “clean ingredient” initiative, which means it’s formulated without ingredients like parabens and phthalates, and is also free of other irritants like fragrance and alcohol, according to the brand. How to shop for colored mascara I asked our experts for advice on how to shop for a colored mascara of your own, including tips on picking a formula for sensitive eyes and ingredients to avoid when shopping. Can you wear colored mascara with sensitive eyes? Those with sensitive eyes don’t have to avoid colored mascara, however our ophthalmologists recommend taking a few precautions. Choose simple, fragrance-free formulas that are also free of potential irritants. You should also avoid waterproof and long-lasting formulas, since they contain additional ingredients.Avoid glitter or shimmer finishes, which can fall easily into your eyes and cause irritation. Those with contact lenses should be especially careful, since they’re more susceptible to flaking formulas, says Zanoni-Potts. Patch-test new products on your inner forearm before buying, to check for texture, flaking etc.Always avoid sharing mascaras, as this can increase the risk of bacteria transfer, says Gill. Are there any mascara ingredients that should be avoided? Dermatologists recommend looking out for (and avoiding) the following mascara ingredients: Both Zanoni-Potts and Gill name fragrance as one of the key culprits to watch out for. It’s one of the most common triggers of allergic and irritant reactions on eyelid skin, which is some of the thinnest skin on the body, says Zanoni-Potts. Depending on your eye sensitivity, you should also avoid formaldehyde-releasing preservatives, says Zanoni-Potts. These can cause contact allergies, especially in those with more sensitive skin. These can include ingredients like quaternium-15, DMDM hydantoin, or imidazolidinyl urea, she says.As mentioned before, loose glitter or glitter-based shimmers in mascara pose a hazard as well, although the hazard is “mechanical rather than chemical,” says Zanoni-Potts. She also recommends steering clear of imported eye cosmetics without a clear FDA labelling, since the regulation of colorants, minerals and heavy metals in eye makeup differs from country to country. articles.title: Why Pakistan is talking to Iran as the Houthi-Saudi fight escalates
articles.summary: Pakistan faces growing pressure to honour its Saudi defence commitments while keeping diplomatic channels to Iran open.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had two phone calls on Thursday night: one with Pakistan’s chief of defence forces, Field Marshal Asim Munir , the other with Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister, Prince Faisal bin Farhan.

The calls capped the most dramatic week yet in the Houthi-Saudi war .

Houthi drones and missiles wounded 73 people and set oil facilities ablaze in four Saudi cities on Tuesday, among the heaviest strikes of the war, according to the Saudi-led coalition.

Iran-backed Houthi fighters reached the coastal town of Mocha at dawn on Thursday and pushed offshore to seize nearby islands . By Friday morning, they had grabbed control of all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Yemeni government officials said fighters also reached Dhubab, on the Bab al-Mandeb coast, while boats carrying Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island , at the heart of the strait, after government forces withdrew.

There has been no official announcement by Houthi authorities confirming control of the strait.

Brent crude surpassed $107 a barrel on Friday, as the advance raised fears that both of Saudi Arabia’s main export routes, the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, could come under pressure at once — one by Iran directly, the other by Tehran’s ally, the Houthis.

Satellite images on Thursday appeared to show a fire along the East-West pipeline, Saudi Arabia’s main Hormuz-bypass route, which carries close to seven million barrels a day over 1,200km (746 miles) to Yanbu.

Riyadh has not confirmed a pipeline strike.

Earlier this week, Pakistan’s Defence Minister, Khawaja Asif, warned that the mutual defence pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye “ will definitely “ be activated if the fighting spills further into the kingdom.

But with Munir calling Tehran on Thursday night, analysts say the question is not whether Pakistan is preparing to act, but whether diplomacy is the course Islamabad has already chosen.

At the Pakistani Foreign Office’s weekly briefing on Thursday, spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan declined to confirm recent reports that Islamabad had passed a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in the Houthis, calling them “unsubstantiated”.

He was equally dismissive of a claim that Saudi Arabia had asked Pakistan to strike Houthi positions in Yemen, calling it “hypothetical” with “no discussion of this kind”.

But when asked whether Pakistan was reaching out to the Houthis through Iran, Khan did not deny it.

Pakistan would “continue to pursue dialogue and diplomacy for peace and stability in the broader region”, Khan said.

Jauhar Saleem, Pakistan’s former foreign secretary and president of the Islamabad-based Institute of Regional Studies, called the phrasing deliberate.

“In diplomacy, what is deliberately not said is as important as what is stated,” he told Al Jazeera, describing Islamabad’s language on the pact as emphasising “deterrence and de-escalation”.

Pakistan’s military chief Munir has travelled to Tehran four times since April. The latest visit came last month, days after a phone call from US President Donald Trump asking Islamabad to lean on Tehran .

An Iranian source familiar with the diplomatic contacts told Al Jazeera that telephone diplomacy has intensified since the escalation began.

“Over the past week to ten days, there have likely been three to four telephone conversations between the Pakistani field marshal and the Iranian foreign minister,” the source said.

“Only two were made public, by the Iranian side,” the source added, describing the rest as in keeping with Islamabad’s preference for “silent diplomacy”.

Al Jazeera received no response from Pakistani officials to questions on the unannounced contacts.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Ishaq Dar, has been speaking separately with his Saudi and Turkish counterparts in recent days.

“The role [as mediator between Saudi Arabia and Iran] fits with the pattern, but with much higher stakes,” Saleem said, arguing that Pakistan’s commitments to Riyadh carry greater risk than its US-Iran mediation ever did.

In April 2015 , its parliament unanimously rejected a Saudi request for troops, ships and warplanes to combat the Houthis, resolving that “Pakistan should maintain neutrality in the Yemen conflict so as to be able to play a proactive diplomatic role to end the crisis”.

Saleem said now “could pose again the dilemma faced by Pakistan’s foreign policy strategists a decade ago, in this very context”.

When Iran struck Saudi Arabia directly in February and March, the kingdom in April announced the arrival of Pakistani forces in Saudi Arabia, even though Islamabad did not directly enter the conflict.

“This shows that the meaning of the mutual-defence principle in the bilateral pact, or the Mecca pact, is a matter calculated by the parties and does not mean the automatic entry of the parties if an attack occurs against the other,” Javad Heiran-Nia, an Iranian analyst on regional security, told Al Jazeera.

The specifics of what Munir and Araghchi spoke about on Thursday night remain unclear.

But analyst Heiran-Nia said Pakistan’s role was clear. “Pakistan has recently conveyed Saudi Arabia’s warning message to Iran and asked Tehran to restrain its Houthi allies,” he told Al Jazeera. “This action demonstrates Pakistan’s active and operational role as a communication channel between the two sides.”

On Tehran’s leverage over the group, he was equally direct.

“Iran has significant influence over the Houthis, although this influence is not absolute and unlimited,” he said. “It is true that the Houthis may in some cases make their decisions independently of Iran, but their strategic interests align with Tehran.”

On Friday, after the Houthis gained control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, Iranian leaders were quick to show where their loyalties lay.

Iran’s First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref welcomed the “victories of the heroic nation of Yemen,” in a post on X.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, was even more direct in claiming influence over the Houthis, as a part of Tehran’s so-called Axis of Resistance.

“Congratulations on this resounding victory, Ansar Allah,” Mokhber posted on X, referring to the Houthis by their formal name. “Iran’s might in the Strait of Hormuz and the homegrown resolve of the resistance have driven the US and its allies into a tactical and strategic impasse.”

Asif Durrani, Pakistan’s former ambassador to Iran and one-time special representative for Afghanistan, framed Pakistan’s position differently.

Under the Mecca pact, he told Al Jazeera, “the major issue is threat perception”, where member states raise concerns and partners respond at the request of the threatened state.

Pakistan, he said, “has the capacity to partner with Saudi Arabia in countering the Houthi threat”.

For the moment, former ambassador Saleem said, “Riyadh does not need Pakistan to fight any battles”. Pakistan could help Saudi Arabia better “by preventing any regional wars,” pointing to Islamabad’s strong ties across the Gulf Cooperation Council and its channels to Tehran.

But Umer Karim, an analyst at Riyadh’s King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies, suggested a moment of reckoning for the Pakistan-Saudi relationship might be approaching.

“The cost of inaction is certainly increasing,” Karim added, “and eventually Pakistan will be pushed to react and fulfil its commitments” under both a bilateral mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and the trilateral agreement that also includes Turkiye.

“Riyadh is probably for now reevaluating the situation and figuring out what’s the best outcome.”

articles.title: Oprah Winfrey audience applauds call to support women without Lindsay Clancy's 'privilege' after mistrial
articles.summary: Oprah Winfrey's podcast audience cheered as a guest urged compassion for women of color imprisoned for crimes similar to the ones in Lindsay Clancy's case.
articles.body: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 800-273-TALK (8255). An audience at a taping of Oprah Winfrey's podcast on Thursday applauded a call to support women like Lindsay Clancy who don't have "her privilege" after Clancy's murder trial ended in a mistrial. Winfrey's show took place in the wake of Clancy's trial after she admitted to strangling her three children in 2023. Last week, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her children. Her defense argued that Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time. ROGAN SHREDS SUPPORTERS OF LINDSAY CLANCY, SAYS THEY WOULDN'T RALLY IF A FATHER WERE ON TRIAL FOR SAME CRIME Winfrey's guests included Dr. Kameelah Phillips, an OB-GYN, who discussed concerns over postpartum psychosis based on how little is known about it. Phillips also encouraged the audience to have compassion not just for Clancy but for "women of color." "And the other thing that I would just be remiss to not say is... I hope this never happens," Phillips said. "We know statistically it really will." "It will," Winfrey replied. "I want us to have the same passion for people who don't look like Lindsay, who don't have her same access," Phillips said. After the audience clapped at her response, Phillips continued, "Who don't have her same access and education, her melanin, her privilege. There are women of color sitting around this country in prisons for this same thing that we've never heard of. And I just want to remind us to have the pink shirts and the energy for them as well." LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL: POSTPARTUM IS REAL, BUT CHILD KILLING DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY, VETERAN PROSECUTOR SAYS Fox News Digital reached out to Winfrey's representatives and Phillips for comment. During the trial, Clancy received the support of hundreds of people outside the courthouse, which drew criticism from some commentators. "We don't see any of them standing out there with a button with the three children's faces on them. When you listen to interviews with all of the women who are standing out, they almost never mention the three child victims," conservative columnist and mother of six Bethany Mandel told Fox News Digital. Dr. Phil McGraw also told "Fox News Live" on Saturday that he was concerned that mental illness in this case has become "kind of a political, ideological football that’s used to try to skew something or is kind of debunked by another side rather than looking at what actually took place." LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER TORCHES CONSPIRACY THEORIES ACCUSING PATRICK CLANCY "I think people underestimate the power of psychosis in taking over someone’s life. It’s not an excuse, but, for example, if she had a brain tumor you could see on an X-ray, people would go ‘OK, I get that.’ And when you have what took place here, it could be just as powerful as someone whose brain is hijacked by a tumor," McGraw said. articles.title: ‘Majority do not welcome him’: Trump heads to Ireland amid fury over Gaza
articles.summary: Protests set to erupt across Ireland, where President Connolly has long regarded the US as an untrustworthy power.
articles.body:
Donald Trump is set to arrive in Ireland on Saturday, but most Irish people aren’t happy about it.

A recent poll by the Sunday Independent and Ireland Thinks reported that 69 percent do not support the US president’s visit.

“Thousands of us will march on Saturday because we refuse to normalise a man who has facilitated genocide,” Sean Radcliffe, an economics undergraduate student at Trinity College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.

Taoiseach Micheal Martin “should say it clearly, firmly, and publicly: the United States is facilitating genocide,” added Radcliffe, who is a leader of the student body’s Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions campaign.

Sean Corcoran, an environmental artist based on the Copper Coast in Waterford, spent five hours with three others carving “No Kings” – a nod to anti-Trump protests under the same name in the US, along with “Gaza, Iran, Ice ,” into the sand of Dublin Bay Beach.

“As an Irish artist and citizen, I believe it is important for me to use my voice to share my opinion about the Trump administration,” he told Al Jazeera. “Despite the diplomatic and security welcome that Mr Trump will receive when he lands in Ireland, the majority of Irish do not welcome him to Ireland.”

Trump is expected to meet with several figures in Ireland’s leadership, including Martin and antiwar President Catherine Connolly, who has previously said the US is, along with France and England, a nation Ireland “certainly cannot trust”.

Protests are planned throughout Ireland, including in Dublin’s Garden of Remembrance. Many are themed against Trump’s role in supporting Israel’s actions in Palestine.

Ireland, one of the West’s most vocal critics of Israel, was the first European Union country to ban imports from illegal Israeli settlements.

Roughly 4,000 security personnel will be enlisted to protect the US leader from protests and other risks during his visit, including roughly 1,000 US Secret Service agents and “anti-drone weaponry”.

Following his visits with Ireland’s political elites and the US ambassador to Ireland, resulting in the temporary shutdown of Phoenix Park, one of Europe’s largest parks, he is expected to visit the Irish Open golf tournament in Doonbeg, where Trump owns a resort.

Connolly, whose role is largely ceremonial, has said that she is “not afraid to stand against the consensus”. She secured a landslide victory in October 2025.

During her campaign, Connolly said she would meet the US president in her official capacity, but added that “I doubt that [genocide] would be the discussion, I doubt that [Gaza] would be on the agenda”.

“People expect a slightly more activist president who might speak out,” Johan Dornschneider-Elkink, professor of Computational Political Science at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera. “The high level of consensus in the Irish population means that the president can also feel a bit comfortable pushing it a bit.”

Still, the limitations of Connolly’s role, and the economic obligations of the taoiseach are expected to overshadow the issue of Palestine during high-level conversations.

‘Ireland is very much aligned in spirit’

“I think [the protest] shows that Ireland is very much aligned in spirit and policy-wise with the Palestinian people; they very much identify with Palestine,” Stephanie Dornschneider-Elkink, associate professor of Political Science at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.

“But there’s also only so much space to be critical. Ireland depends on the US, and there’s an economic relationship at stake.”

Johan added that the visit is more an opportunity for Irish people who want to make known their stance on both Palestine and the Trump administration.

“There’s an understanding that Trump is one president among many, and there will be another president. There’s a longer history of the Irish-US relationship which nobody wants to see damaged.”

Leader of the Opposition Mary Lou McDonald of Sinn Fein, told journalists this week that she hoped Connolly would raise issues like “ongoing facilitation of a genocide in Gaza,” adding that the party will take part in Saturday’s protests.

The party’s spokesperson on foreign affairs, trade, and defence, Donnchadh O Laoghaire TD, shared on his Instagram that he would join the protest in the Garden of Remembrance, asking others to join him “to stand up against genocide and against war”.

The demonstration is organised by the Irish Neutrality League, in coalition with the Irish Anti-War Movement and social justice movement Tonn na Cle, and has received endorsements from the Social Democrats, Labour, People Before Profit-Solidarity, and the Green Party, in addition to Sinn Fein.

Student groups in Ireland have been among the loudest voices of pro-Palestine organising in the country, with Trinity College Dublin becoming the first university in the world to officially sever ties with Israel.

Radcliffe said there is no generational divide “of any significance” over the Israel-Palestine conflict in Ireland.

“Some of the best [pro-Palestine] activists I know in Ireland are pensioners,” he said.

articles.title: Gel Manicures are Now Banned in the UK and Europe: Here’s What to Know
articles.summary: The UK has banned certain gel nail polishes. Here’s what you need to know about the potential dangers of a gel manicure.
articles.body: Last summer, the European Union, which is made up of 27 nations including France, Spain, Italy and more, made headlines when they banned an ingredient called Trimethylbenzoyl Diphenylphosphine Oxide (TPO), which is commonly used in many gel nail polishes. Now, the United Kingdom, a non-EU country, has officially followed suit — as of August 22, TPO is no longer allowed in UK nail salons. Europe is known for being quite strict when it comes to regulations on beauty products. For example, they don’t allow any animal testing for cosmetics, there is a list of over 1,700 ingredients that are fully banned and marketing claims have to be proven and substantiated by evidence. If you live in the United States, you won’t be impacted by this ban and gel polish containing TPO will continue to be widely available. Even still, this news may give you pause — if Europe is banning this ingredient, should we be staying away from it, too? To answer that very question, we turned to two dermatologists. But first, read more about this reasoning for this ban overseas. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What is Trimethylbenzoyl Diphenylphosphine Oxide (TPO)? Trimethylbenzoyl Diphenylphosphine Oxide (TPO) is a photoinitiator — a fancy word for a molecule that absorbs UV or visible light and generates a reaction of some sort. In the case of TPO, that reaction is a curing or hardening. “In polish, when [TPO] is activated by UV light, it hardens the product on the nail and forms a film,” says Dr. Jeffrey S. Fromowitz, a board-certified dermatologist and medical director and managing partner at Dermatology of Boca in Boca Raton, Florida. In the beauty world this ingredient is really only used in gel nail polish. Outside of that, you can find it in certain adhesives, sealants and inks. Why did Europe ban certain gel nail polishes? The European Union, and more recently the UK, banned TPO because animal studies done on rats associated it with negative reproductive outcomes for males. One thing to know: The rats were repeatedly fed high doses of TPO — much more than one would be exposed to via a gel manicure. Because of these findings, as of September 1, 2025 in Europe and August 22, 2026 in the United Kingdom, no gel nail polish containing TPO can be sold. On top of that, European nail technicians must immediately stop using polish they have that contains TPO. It’s helpful to know that regulations set forth by the European Union and the UK are typically more strict because they are based on potential risks, which may or may not be seen in a real-world setting, says Fromowitz. In this case, the conditions in these animal settings do not mimic real world usage and no studies have been done on humans to determine if TPO is actually dangerous, which is why the United States Food and Drug Administration is unlikely to ban them. Is it safe to use gel nail polish with TPO? Again, the European Union and the United Kingdom have banned TPO because they believe there is potential risk to the reproductive system. “It is believed to be an endocrine disruptor (harmful to reproduction),” says Dr. Allison Leer, a board-certified dermatologist and co-founder of Botanist Nails. “Endocrine disruptors have the potential to interfere with the body’s hormone system which can have adverse effects such as reduced fertility and birth defects.” Again, while it is possible, there really isn’t much proof that using TPO can cause issues with infertility since there have been zero studies done looking for risks in humans, says Fromowitz. Given this, it’s really up to you whether you want to cease using gel nail polish that contains TPO. 5 TPO-free nail polishes to consider Looking for an alternative to gel polish with TPO? “Traditional nail polish doesn’t require a UV light and there are many non-toxic formulas available,” says Leer. Below, we rounded up a handful of TPO-free polishes. We prioritized options that provide a similar long-lasting effect and that have high ratings. This four step nail system gives you the look of a gel mani without the UV light and polish that contains TPO. You start with the brand’s nail prep to remove any oils or lotions from your nails, then layer on a base coat, the polish and a top coat. Everything dries within five minutes and the manicure will last up to seven days, according to the brand. This kit has all the products you need, including a bottle of the brand’s polish in their Rapid Red color. This polish gives nails mega shine, similar to a gel polish. It is intended to be paired with the brand’s gel-like top coat to make your manicure last up to 8 days, according to Sally Hansen. It is available in 22 colors on Amazon, including sheer and sparkly options. This two-step polish set from Essie comes with a color (choose from 23 shades) and a top coat that gives you a super glossy finish. To get a manicure that lasts as long as possible, apply two coats of the color and then top with the gel-like top coat and let it dry completely. The brush on this polish is also shaped in a special way to easily cover the edges nicely, according to the brand. The set has a 4.6-star average rating from over 11,150 reviews on Amazon. “Press-on nails are also a good alternative to gel polish,” says Leer. “If applied correctly they look very similar to a manicure and they don’t damage your natural nails.” These press-ons from Glamnetic come in over 40 colors, designs and nail shapes — allowing you to really customize nails to suit your needs and wants. They come with easy-to-apply glue and will last up to two weeks, according to the brand. Don’t like the feeling of press-ons? These nail stickers give you a similar look but feel a bit more like polish sitting on your nail. There are 28 nail strips in varying sizes included, so you can find the perfect fit for your hands. The set also comes with a prep pad, nail file and wooden stick. There are fifteen designs available and they have a 4.2-star average rating from over 540 reviews on Amazon. articles.title: Ebola case detected in seventh DR Congo province
articles.summary: Case found in northwestern province of South-Ubangi bordering the Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville.
articles.body:
The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached a seventh province bordering the Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville, according to local authorities.

The acting governor of the northwestern province of South-Ubangi, Jean-Rene Galekwa Vundawe, issued a statement on Friday saying Ebola was detected following laboratory analysis of a suspected case in the province.

Jean-Jacques Muyembe, head of DRC’s National Institute for Biomedical Research in Kinshasa, confirmed that a man had tested positive for Ebola.

Until now, the Bundibugyo virus, the rare kind of Ebola that caused the current outbreak, had been in six provinces in the country’s east and northeast. Local transmission has not yet been confirmed in South-Ubangi, meaning it ⁠has not been added to ⁠the list of provinces officially affected by the epidemic.

The outbreak, DRC’s 17th, is already the deadliest and the biggest in the country’s history in terms of case numbers – a milestone reached in late July.

As of Wednesday, 6,942 cases and 3,349 deaths have been reported, according to the latest government figures, well above the 2,299 deaths recorded in DRC’s 2018-2020 outbreak of the Zaire Ebola virus, previously the country’s worst on record.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has said the current outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak across West Africa, which killed more than 11,325 people, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

Friday’s statement by the South-Ubangi governor’s office said a sample from a patient in the Bulu health district was tested by DRC’s national research institute, and laboratory results found the presence of the Bundibugyo virus.

The patient who died in South-Ubangi had developed symptoms in the capital of Tshopo province, Kisangani, where Ebola cases have been reported, after travelling through Rwanda, Uganda and Ituri province in northeastern DRC, Galekwa said. The patient then travelled by boat on the Congo River.

“The route taken both by the patient and by the boat exposes the populations” of the provinces of North-Ubangi, Tshopo and Mongala, Galekwa said.

“Thirty-eight people have been identified as having been in contact with the patient and have been placed in quarantine,” he said.

In recent weeks, new cases and deaths have declined in Ituri province, the outbreak’s epicentre, but risen sharply in neighbouring North Kivu and Upper-Uele.

The Bundibugyo variant of Ebola currently has no approved vaccines or treatments.

However, several treatments and vaccines are being tested.

The outbreak has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15, as weak health infrastructure, the region’s remoteness, and ongoing conflict near DRC’s borders with South Sudan, Uganda and Rwanda have hindered efforts to respond to cases.

articles.title: About 4,000 years ago, builders hauled 25-tonne stones 11 miles across northern England to create the ‘Devil’s Arrows’, Britain’s tallest surviving prehistoric stone row
articles.summary: UK News: The Devil’s Arrows, Britain’s tallest surviving prehistoric stone row, have long raised questions about where they came from and how they reached Boro.
articles.body: The Devil’s Arrows, Britain’s tallest surviving prehistoric stone row, have long raised questions about where they came from and how they reached Boroughbridge. It turns out that ancient Neolithic builders hauled these enormous 25-tonne structures across at least 11 miles to get there.Researchers at the University of York and Curtin University in Australia have shed new light on these prehistoric stones in Yorkshire. Further geological analyses revealed that Neolithic people bypassed more local stone sources to bring the giant megaliths from Brimham Rocks in North Yorkshire, settling a long debate over whether humans or Ice Age glaciers moved them.The researchers also confirmed that a missing stone is hiding in plain sight in the nearby village of Aldborough, in the form of a cross, proving 19th-century theories and local legends to be true. The findings are published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A.Yorkshire's Neolithic labour of legendThe Devil's Arrows, as locals call them, rise almost seven metres (23ft) high, making these three surviving pillars near Boroughbridge the tallest standing stone row in Britain. They are even taller than the stones at Stonehenge. The southern stone is the second-tallest standing stone in Britain, after the Rudston Monolith, while the central stone is the third-tallest. For long, scientists wondered how these stones arrived. The researchers used isotopic ‘fingerprinting’ to show that the stones came from Brimham Rocks, 11 miles (18km) away. This proves that the builders were intentional about choosing stones from a distant place instead of using closer sources.“Megalithic architecture is among the most visually striking features of the Neolithic landscape across Britain and Ireland, from vast ceremonial complexes like Avebury and Stonehenge to individual standing stones. Sites in southern England and Scotland receive considerable attention, but monuments like the Devil's Arrows have remained comparatively understudied despite their significance,” Dr Jim Leary, from the University of York’s Department of Archaeology, said.“We have now proved that Neolithic communities moved several 25-tonne stones 18km across Yorkshire, transforming a familiar site into an epic quest to create a sacred landscape,” he added.In the mid-16th century, Tudor antiquarian John Leland recorded a fourth standing stone; however, decades later, it went missing. By 1687, records said locals had broken up the fallen stone, used part of it to construct Peg Bridge over the River Tutt and taken the top segment to Aldborough Manor.Later in the 19th century, antiquarian J.R. Walbran proposed that another fallen monolith had been used to make the Battle Cross, a 5.5-metre monument crafted in the 15th century to commemorate the 1322 Battle of Boroughbridge.The new study confirmed Walbran’s theory. The mineral fingerprinting found that the medieval cross standing in Aldborough today is indeed a carved segment of a long-lost Arrow.The Devil's Arrows stand on Triassic Sherwood Sandstone; however, the monoliths themselves are made of Pennine Basin Millstone Grit, a different type of coarse-grained sandstone formed during the Namurian period over 300 million years ago.“While the nearest gritstone outcrops sit just 5km west of Boroughbridge, and long-suspected alternative sources like Plumpton Rocks sit 13km away, we used high-resolution isotopic testing of microscopic zircon and apatite minerals to trace their exact geological birthplace,” Dr Anthony Clarke, geochemist at Curtin University in Australia, said.“By mapping the unique mineral age profiles locked inside the stone, we proved the megaliths were quarried 18km away at Brimham Rocks, ruling out the idea that they were local glacial rocks left behind by ice sheets,” he added.On the western edge of Boroughbridge, the three surviving stones are spaced unevenly across 174 metres. Historic evidence suggests that the site once held at least five stones, and likely more, standing on gently sloping ground near a possible prehistoric ford on the River Ure. They formed the southern gateway to an enormous sacred landscape between the Rivers Swale and Ure, anchoring a region dotted with seven late-Neolithic henges, the densest concentration in Britain.“The Devil’s Arrows have inspired stories and sparked curiosity for generations. Local legend tells of the Devil standing on How Hill and hurling giant stone arrows towards Boroughbridge, only for them to fall short and land where they stand today. While the folklore remains a much-loved part of their story, it’s wonderful to discover that the real journey of these stones is every bit as extraordinary,” Justin Scully, General Manager for Fountains Abbey & Studley Royal and Brimham Rocks, said.“This fascinating research reveals a direct link between Brimham Rocks and the Devil’s Arrows, connecting two remarkable Yorkshire landscapes in our care. We’re incredibly grateful to the researchers for helping us uncover this new chapter in the stones’ story and deepen our understanding of the people who shaped this landscape thousands of years ago,” Scully added.Jess Tipper, Historic England's North Region Inspector of Ancient Monuments, reflected, “The Devil's Arrows are a much-loved part of Boroughbridge's rich heritage and we're delighted these scientific discoveries add to the understanding of their history. And we look forward to finding out more about them and how we can protect them for everyone to enjoy.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
